title: Challenge: Peak Binary Search

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only peak-search program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
A peak exists on that side under the unequal-neighbor contract. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[3,2,1]`, the worked program returns `0`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[1,2,3,1]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Parse a nonempty array with unequal adjacent values. Return any strict peak index, treating outside endpoint values as negative infinity.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Parse a nonempty array with unequal adjacent values. Return any strict peak index, treating outside endpoint values as negative infinity. On input `[1,2,3,1]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Compare adjacent slopes; one side is guaranteed to contain a peak. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. Binary search maintains an interval that is still capable of containing the answer. State precisely why the discarded half cannot contain it. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(log n) time · O(1) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Check no match, duplicate matches, the first and last valid positions, and an answer at the boundary of the search domain. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `0`. A peak exists on that side under the unequal-neighbor contract. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: In [1,2,3,1], the comparison at index 1 rises toward index 2. The next comparison falls from 3 to 1, retaining index 2. Outside the endpoints is treated as negative infinity; an endpoint may be a valid peak.
